````math
## Appendix E Analysis of Tool Scoring

The following diagnostics examine the evidence used by the score, the
attribution rule, and the stability of the aggregate ranking. They use
different scopes to isolate these choices: request-level selection,
pooled configurations across TGB families, and the task-specific spaces
of the main experiments. Request-level thresholding retains tools above
a tuned threshold $`\tau^{\star}`$; support-frequency retention uses the
rule defined in
Appendix [D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Do Further Updates Improve an Existing Space? ‣ Appendix D Tool-Space Construction and Subsequent Updates ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization"),
with an explicitly reported exception for Llama-3.1-8B. Results from
different scopes are not treated as matched comparisons.

### E.1 Top-$`K`$ Selection as Surrogate Maximization

LOTS measures each tool’s contribution with the other tools present,
then selects a task-specific space from the resulting scores. This
section restates Theorem 1 of
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Task-Level Tool-Space Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization")
with its setting and proof: the selection exactly optimizes an additive
approximation to the fixed-output likelihood objective. Bounded tool
interactions then give an explicit bound on the approximation error and
the resulting selection gap. Consider one task and a fixed collection of
requests $`Q`$ served under a common tool menu $`S`$, with $`m=|S|`$.
For each request $`x`$, keep its recorded output $`y_{x}`$ fixed. Let
$`h_{x}(A)`$ denote the scoring context obtained by retaining the
evidence associated with $`A\subseteq S`$, using a fixed intervention
rule and leaving tool documentation unchanged. Define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F(A)=\frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{x\in Q}\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(y_{x}\mid h_{x}(A)).
``` |  | (10) |

Thus, $`F`$ measures support for the recorded outputs, rather than the
accuracy of newly generated answers. The task-averaged LOTS score is

|     |                               |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       I(s)=F(S)-F(S\setminus\{s\}).
       ```                            |     | (11) |

These scores define the additive approximation

|     |                                                   |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{F}(A)=F(S)-\sum_{s\in S\setminus A}I(s).
       ```                                                |     | (12) |

It agrees exactly with $`F`$ at the full menu and at every single-tool
deletion. Since
$`\widehat{F}(A)=F(S)-\sum_{s\in S}I(s)+\sum_{s\in A}I(s)`$, retaining
the $`K`$ highest-scoring tools exactly maximizes $`\widehat{F}(A)`$
subject to $`|A|=K`$. The approximation arises only when several tools
are removed together: their joint effect need not equal the sum of their
individual leave-one-out effects.

Tool interactions. Following the discrete-difference formulation of
set-function interactions ([Sundararajan et al., 2020](#bib.bib38)),
define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{s,t}F(B)=F(B\cup\{s,t\})-F(B\cup\{s\})-F(B\cup\{t\})+F(B),
``` |  | (13) |

for distinct $`s,t\notin B`$. This quantity measures how the presence of
one tool changes the marginal contribution of the other. Positive values
indicate complementarity in the likelihood objective; negative values
indicate substitutability. The following result bounds the error of the
LOTS approximation using these interactions.

Theorem 1 (selection under bounded interactions). Fix a budget $`K`$ and
let $`r=m-K`$. Suppose that, for some $`\beta\geq 0`$,

|     |                             |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       |\Delta_{s,t}F(B)|\leq\beta
       ```                          |     | (14) |

for every $`B\subseteq S`$ with $`K\leq|B|\leq m-2`$ and every distinct
$`s,t\in S\setminus B`$. Then every set $`A`$ of size $`K`$ satisfies

|     |                                             |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       |F(A)-\widehat{F}(A)|\leq\binom{r}{2}\beta.
       ```                                          |     | (15) |

Let $`A_{\mathrm{LOTS}}`$ contain the $`K`$ highest-scoring tools, and
let $`A^{\star}\in\arg\max_{|A|=K}F(A)`$. Then

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       0\leq F(A^{\star})-F(A_{\mathrm{LOTS}})\leq r(r-1)\beta.
       ```                                                       |     | (16) |

Proof. For any $`A`$ with $`|A|=K`$, order the removed tools as
$`S\setminus A=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{r}\}`$. Set $`S_{0}=S`$ and
$`S_{i}=S_{i-1}\setminus\{d_{i}\}`$. The likelihood loss at deletion
$`i`$ is

|     |                               |     |
|-----|-------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \ell_{i}=F(S_{i-1})-F(S_{i}).
       ```                            |     |

Its difference from the full-context score $`I(d_{i})`$ comes from the
preceding $`i-1`$ deletions. Each preceding deletion changes this
marginal by a second-order difference of the form
equation [13](#A5.E13 "In E.1 Top-𝐾 Selection as Surrogate Maximization ‣ Appendix E Analysis of Tool Scoring ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization").
All corresponding contexts have sizes between $`K`$ and $`m-2`$, so the
assumption gives

|     |                                    |     |
|-----|------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       |\ell_{i}-I(d_{i})|\leq(i-1)\beta.
       ```                                 |     |

Telescoping the deletion losses yields

|     |                                   |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       F(A)=F(S)-\sum_{i=1}^{r}\ell_{i}.
       ```                                |     |

Consequently,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
|F(A)-\widehat{F}(A)|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}|\ell_{i}-I(d_{i})|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{r}(i-1)\beta=\binom{r}{2}\beta.
``` |  |

Write $`\delta=\binom{r}{2}\beta`$. Because $`A_{\mathrm{LOTS}}`$
maximizes $`\widehat{F}`$ among sets of size $`K`$,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
F(A^{\star})\leq\widehat{F}(A^{\star})+\delta\leq\widehat{F}(A_{\mathrm{LOTS}})+\delta\leq F(A_{\mathrm{LOTS}})+2\delta,
``` |  |

which proves the selection bound. For $`r=0`$ or $`r=1`$, the
approximation is exact. $`\square`$

The bound requires that a tool’s marginal contribution not change
sharply as other tools are removed; each interaction in
equation [13](#A5.E13 "In E.1 Top-𝐾 Selection as Surrogate Maximization ‣ Appendix E Analysis of Tool Scoring ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization")
costs four fixed-output evaluations, so sampled pairs can test it. The
analysis covers one common-menu batch and the fixed-output objective,
not running scores across menus or execution accuracy.

### E.3 Deletion Operation in the Leave-One-Out Score

On TGB, removing $`s`$ re-executes the chain, so a downstream tool that
needs $`s`$’s output returns an error. We compare this *re-execute*
deletion with *evidence only*, which deletes just the recorded output
line of $`s`$, on the same 80 fitting requests per family, the same
traces and the same frozen answers (Qwen2.5-7B).

1.56 9 / 9 66.6 71.4 72.3

Table 18: Two deletion operations on Qwen2.5-7B: chain identification on
the fitting requests and evaluation accuracy of the spaces they select
at fixed budgets. The mean rank is over the chain tools of the nine

Both deletions place the complete chain of every tool-using family
within its top $`|G|`$ positions, their pooled scores correlate at 0.91,
the top-4 sets agree in all ten families and the top-2 sets in nine, and
the deployed accuracy is identical at $`K=4`$ and $`K=8`$ and differs by
0.2 points at $`K=2`$. Evidence-only deletion halves the upstream scores
(DocRetrieve in fx_settle 1.21 to 0.87, SensorAPI in sensor_mean 1.86 to
0.55), because the recorded downstream output still carries the upstream
information; the mean upstream rank moves from 1.11 to 1.56 and
Calculator moves above ExchangeRate in fx_settle. Re-execution credits
an upstream tool with its effect through its dependents, the quantity a
deployment removes when it drops the tool.

### E.4 From Likelihood Scores to Execution Utility

For each of eight models and ten TGB families, the scores cached from
the first 80 requests select the $`K`$ highest-scoring tools (Top-$`K`$)
and one random subset of the same size, evaluated on the remaining 320
requests. Excluding no_tool, seven models separate the reference-chain
tools from the rest with an AUROC of 1.000 on all nine families and
Gemma4-12B with 0.992, so 71 of 72 model–family pairs are separated
perfectly. In

Top-$`K`$ beats Random and Keep all on every model, averaging 0.819
against 0.222 and 0.694: the ranking, not the size of the space, carries
the gain.

### E.5 Scoring Models, Aggregation, and Incorrect Outputs

Rescoring the same instruct-model traces and frozen outputs with the
base model, then serving with the instruct model, selects the same tools
for Qwen2.5-14B, Mistral-7B and Qwen3-4B and gives higher accuracy for
the other three models
(Figure [17](#A5.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ E.5 Scoring Models, Aggregation, and Incorrect Outputs ‣ Appendix E Analysis of Tool Scoring ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization")).
The instruct scorer is closer to the gold chain on five of six models,
and base scores are smaller on five, so fewer tools pass the fixed
threshold of the support-frequency rule used here; at a fixed $`K`$,
top-$`K`$ selection is invariant to a uniform rescaling of the scores.

Figure 17: Scoring-model diagnostic on TGB: accuracy under Keep all and
under the spaces fitted with an instruct-model or a base-model scorer,
from frozen instruct-model outputs and a fixed support-frequency
threshold. The instruct model serves every configuration; the right
margin gives the number of tools each scorer keeps.

Incorrect outputs and aggregation.

uses pooled configurations fitted from 3,000 traces per model and
evaluated on 400 separate requests, with correct-only and wrong-only
subsets and synthetic corruption of a random fraction of the scored

the correct-only and wrong-only rankings correlate at Spearman 0.911;

## Appendix F Computational Cost and Registry Scaling

A trace with $`m`$ interventions needs at most $`m+1`$ teacher-forced
sequences, one with the full context and one per intervention; no
replacement answer is generated.
Table [20](#A6.T20 "Table 20 ‣ Appendix F Computational Cost and Registry Scaling ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization")
reports selection and serving input tokens: the GTA-Atomic fit scores 33
requests over seven candidates (264 sequences) at fixed $`K=2`$, and the
BFCL rows use the 101-record tune protocol at fixed $`K=16`$. A router
pays its selection call on every request; a frozen space pays once. The
full-menu runs that produced the fitting traces are excluded from the
selection column; charging them adds about 98k prompt tokens on
GTA-Atomic and 29M on BFCL. Serving tokens count every agent turn. On
GTA-Atomic the 14-tool schema has 2,147 tokens and the OCR+Calculator
schema 186, and Qwen2.5-7B processes 2,956 against 1,572 prompt tokens
per request; the size-matched random menu uses 671 tokens but also makes
fewer calls. On TGB, serving under the fitted spaces uses 143 to 181
prompt tokens per request against 251 to 319 for the full fifteen-tool
menu, 33 to 46% fewer.

For a frozen configuration with fitting cost $`C_{\mathrm{fit}}`$ and
per-request serving costs $`c_{\mathrm{full}}>c_{\mathrm{space}}`$, the
break-even count is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
N_{\mathrm{break}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{fit}}}{c_{\mathrm{full}}-c_{\mathrm{space}}}.
``` |  | (17) |

Figure [20](#A6.F20 "Figure 20 ‣ Appendix F Computational Cost and Registry Scaling ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization")
plots this account for GTA-Atomic; token break-even differs from latency
break-even, since teacher-forced scoring, cached prefill and decoding
cost different amounts per token. A deployment that keeps updating also
pays for later scoring rounds, so over $`R`$ rounds the total is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{\mathrm{total}}=\sum_{k=0}^{R-1}\left(C_{\mathrm{serve},k}+C_{\mathrm{score},k}+C_{\mathrm{extra\ trace},k}\right),
``` |  | (18) |

and
Table [12](#A4.T12 "Table 12 ‣ D.4 Constructing Spaces as New Task Types Arrive ‣ Appendix D Tool-Space Construction and Subsequent Updates ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization")
reports the serving component only.

Figure [21](#A6.F21 "Figure 21 ‣ F.1 Scaling with Registry Size ‣ Appendix F Computational Cost and Registry Scaling ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization")
appends synthetic distractors to the 15-tool registry; two rounds each
serve 400 requests from all ten families, the second under one pooled
configuration fitted from the first. Full-menu accuracy falls from 0.677
at 15 tools to 0.508 at 120 on Qwen2.5-7B, where the fitted 43-tool
configuration reaches 0.598; Qwen3.5-9B’s fitted configurations keep
about seven tools and average 0.607, 0.612, 0.594, and 0.538 over four

0.446 to 0.345;
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Agents via Likelihood-Guided Tool-Space Optimization")(c)
plots these means. Scoring time grows from 176 seconds at 15 tools to
8,158 seconds at 120 on one L40S, and to 3,437 seconds under the fitted
configuration.
````
